analysis.one_liner: Forces employers to run written safety programs, gives workers safety committees, and extends OSHA to government workers.
analysis.headline: A sweeping workplace-safety bill with 136 cosponsors cleared the House Education and Labor Committee in July 1992, but it never received a vote on the House floor before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the nation's main workplace-safety law. It required every employer to write and follow a safety program, gave employees at larger workplaces the right to safety committees that can inspect the site and see injury records, sped up and stiffened standards and penalties, protected workers who report hazards or refuse dangerous work, and extended federal safety coverage for the first time to state, local, and most federal employees. The House committee approved it after months of hearings, but no floor vote ever happened.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at hazardous jobs, who would get guaranteed safety programs, committees with the right to inspect worksites quarterly and see injury records, protection from being fired for reporting injuries or refusing dangerous work, and faster government action on toxic exposures. Roughly 7 million state and local government workers would gain federal OSHA protection for the first time, along with workers at Department of Energy nuclear facilities.

how_it_helps.text: Requires each employer to maintain a written safety and health program that identifies hazards, corrects them, and trains workers, with training counted as paid work time [S2].

Requires employers with 11 or more employees to establish safety and health committees that can inspect the worksite at least quarterly, review injury records, and accompany government inspectors, with no loss of pay for that time [S2].

Extends OSHA coverage to state and local government employees and to most federal workers, including Department of Energy nuclear facilities, closing a gap that left millions of public workers uncovered [S2].

Sets deadlines for the Labor Department to act on toxic-exposure limits and requires an ergonomics standard to prevent musculoskeletal injuries, with court review available if the Secretary delays [S2] [S4].

Raises criminal penalties for willful violations causing death to up to 20 years, creates felony penalties for willful violations causing serious injury, and bars officers from having the employer pay their personal fines [S4].

Extends anti-retaliation protection to workers who report injuries or unsafe conditions, lengthens the complaint window from 30 to 180 days, and allows compensatory damages and attorney's fees for workers who are fired for speaking up [S2].
Grants injured workers and families of killed workers rights to meet with investigators, get copies of citations, and speak before any settlement that weakens a citation [S2] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Employers bear the cost: writing and running safety programs, paying committee members for time spent on safety duties, paying higher penalties (up to $50,000 per day for ignoring an imminent-danger notice), and facing personal criminal exposure for willful violations. State and local governments become regulated employers too. Compliance costs would ultimately show up in prices and government budgets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employers and state and local governments

drawbacks.text: Every employer with 11 or more employees would have to maintain written programs, run committees, and provide recurring paid training, a substantial administrative and cost burden that falls hardest on small firms' paperwork rather than on hazards that may not exist at a given site [S2] [S3].

The bill mandates a detailed ergonomics standard and rapid deadlines for many specific standards within one to three years, an ambitious timetable that regulators might struggle to meet with sound science [S4].

Criminal exposure extends to certain officers, managers, and supervisors for willful violations, and penalties of $10,000-$50,000 per day for continued exposure to a posted imminent danger are severe enough that even supporters would acknowledge a risk of disputed or overbroad citations [S3] [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits were broad and concrete: mandatory hazard programs, worker participation rights, coverage for millions of uncovered public employees, and penalties that finally made willful violations of safety law a serious crime. The costs were real but ordinary regulatory compliance costs, concentrated on employers, and the bill gave the Secretary authority to ease requirements where risks were low. The main design criticism is the rushed timetable for numerous standards and the paperwork load on small employers.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee spent nearly a year on hearings and approved the bill on July 9, 1992, but no one ever brought it to the House floor for a vote, and the Congress ended in January 1993 with the bill dead.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on August 1, 1991 by Rep. William Ford of Michigan and referred to the Education and Labor and Post Office and Civil Service committees [S6].
It drew 136 cosponsors, 135 Democrats and 1 Independent [S5].
The committee held seven rounds of hearings between September 1991 and April 1992 [S6].
The Labor Department submitted an unfavorable executive comment in April 1992, and the Department of Energy did so in May 1992 [S6].
The committee ordered the bill reported in amended form on May 28, 1992, and reported it with House Report 102-663, Part I on July 9, 1992 [S6].
No further House action was taken; the bill never received a floor vote and died when the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced new programs, committees, higher penalties, and personal criminal liability for safety violations are better off because the bill never became law. Workers, including the millions of public employees who would have gained OSHA coverage for the first time, remain under the weaker pre-1991 rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers, and the Bush-era Labor Department position

for.name: Rep. William D. Ford
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through the Education and Labor Committee, which he saw reported in amended form on July 9, 1992.

for.name: House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Held seven sets of hearings, marked the bill up, ordered it reported amended on May 28, 1992, and reported it on July 9, 1992.

against.name: Secretary of Labor
against.what_they_did: Submitted unfavorable executive comment on the bill in April 1992.

against.name: Department of Energy
against.what_they_did: Submitted unfavorable executive comment on May 28, 1992.

against.name: House Democratic leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the committee-approved bill for a floor vote during the remainder of the 102nd Congress.

against.name: Business groups opposed to OSHA expansion
against.what_they_did: Opposed the expansion of employer mandates, committees, and penalties during the 1992 OSHA reform debate.

sides.party_line_note: All 136 cosponsors were Democrats or the one Independent, with no Republican support on the list, and the bill died without ever facing a floor vote where a partisan split could be measured [S5].

industries.industry: Private employers with 11 or more employees
industries.note: The bill imposed mandatory safety programs, worker committees with inspection rights, abatement verification, much higher civil penalties, and felony exposure for willful violations causing injury. Those costs are the flip side of the protections workers would have gained, so the industry's interest in defeating the bill ran against workers' safety.

The bill extended federal OSHA coverage to public employees for the first time, making states and cities regulated employers subject to inspections and penalties. Public workers, who were previously uncovered, would have gained the protections.

industries.industry: Department of Energy and its nuclear facility contractors
industries.note: The bill removed DOE's exemption and put its nuclear facility workers under OSHA, and DOE responded with an unfavorable executive comment. Workers at those facilities would have gained standard OSHA enforcement.

industries.industry: Occupational safety training and consulting providers
industries.note: Mandatory written programs, committee training, and annual refresher courses would have created demand for training materials and services, which the bill directed the Labor Department to help develop.
